node.label: Philippa Levine
node.date_label: The Amateur and the Professional (1986) · “Orientalist Sociology and the Creation of Colonial Sexualities” (2000) · Prostitution, Race and Politics (2003) · Gender and Empire: edited collection (2004)
node.description: A historian of race, sex, science and the British Empire. Her primary article on colonial sexualities examines how official counting, classification and regulation constructed distinctions among women. It connects purportedly empirical social knowledge with racial hierarchy and gendered respectability, while showing that the category of prostitution itself resisted stable legal definition. The entry preserves the difference between her authored monographs and her edited Gender and Empire collection; its other chapters are not assigned to her.

named_group_routes.relationship: Englishness as a formation of class, gender and race: imperial men, masculinities and “raced” white subjects (2002–2003)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Her own retrospective statement, read by the second research pass (JBS 42:4, 2003): her task was "to analyze the 'racing,' to use Toni Morrison's term, of white subjects, the ways in which Englishness needs to be understood not only as a formation of class and of gender, but also of race and ethnicity" (p. 531); the book "is about men, masculinities, and the making of 'raced' subjects" (p. 536); she concedes to Holt and Levine that "There is undoubtedly more that I could have done with the women" (pp. 536–537). Civilising Subjects itself is unread. Distinct from the 1987 Family Fortunes contribution, which reaches gender history through edge_757's social-history claim and the existing roster row.

sources.title: Catherine Hall, “A Response to the Commentators,” Journal of British Studies 42, no. 4 (October 2003): 530–538.
sources.citation: Catherine Hall, “A Response to the Commentators,” Journal of British Studies 42, no. 4 (October 2003): 530–538.

verification.note: Read in part (pp. 530–537; p. 538 not reached) by the second research pass for revision 1.144 (data/extension-2026/post2000-wave1-2026-10-17/evidence-hall.pass2.md §1), in the UCL Discovery open copy. p. 530: "The central argument of Civilising Subjects is that being a colonizer was part of the construction of Englishness in the nineteenth century"; "my task as an historian, as I defined it at the end of the 1980s, was to explore Englishness as a racial formation"; "Yet if, as Frantz Fanon argued, colonialism shaped the colonizers as much as the colonized then how was this expressed in everyday culture? How was it lived 'at home' as well as in the empire?"; the national story, the "island story", challenged by race politics. p. 531: "to analyze the 'racing,' to use Toni Morrison's term, of white subjects, the ways in which Englishness needs to be understood not only as a formation of class and of gender, but also of race and ethnicity". p. 533: "as C. L. R. James's The Black Jacobins (1938) taught us, much can be gained through the analysis of metropole and colony in one lens." p. 534: splitting the narrative meant "reasserting the gap between metropole and colony as fundamental to the maintenance of metropolitan power". pp. 536–537: the book "is about men, masculinities, and the making of 'raced' subjects"; "There is undoubtedly more that I could have done with the women". p. 537: "the well-established narrative of British history, the national history, the one taught in schools and universities, needed to be rethought through the frame of empire." The commentators' texts (Gikandi, Levine, Holt) are unread.

Class/nationality and paternalism are his contested interpretation. Acknowledgments explicitly credit Rawick, Levine, Litwack, Fogel/Engerman and Elizabeth Fox-Genovese; these do not establish coauthorship or agreement. No complete book or direct Gramsci passage read. White-transcribed dialect and master/slave analogies are not independently validated.
